theory.intro: A graph is **planar** if it *can* be drawn on a flat page with no two edges crossing. The word describes the **network**, not one particular picture of it, so a drawing full of crossings tells you nothing on its own — you must ask whether the same vertices and edges can be rearranged so that the crossings disappear. When a planar graph is drawn with no crossings, the edges cut the page into separate regions called **faces**. Every region counts, including the single unbounded region stretching away outside the drawing — the **outer face**. Two networks can never be drawn without crossings no matter how they are rearranged: $K_5$, in which five vertices are each joined to all four of the others, and $K_{3,3}$, in which each of three vertices is joined to each of three others (the three-utilities network). These are the two standard non-planar graphs.
facts: A graph is **planar** if it can be redrawn so that no two edges cross.
Crossings in one drawing do **not** make a graph non-planar — the graph is planar as long as **some** drawing has no crossings.
A redraw must keep **exactly the same vertices and exactly the same edges**; adding, removing or re-routing a connection makes it a different network.
A **face** is a region of the page bounded by edges, and the **outer (infinite) region is always counted as a face**.
An edge that encloses nothing — such as an edge to a vertex of degree $1$ — adds no new face; a **loop** does enclose a region, so it adds one.
Adding one new edge between two vertices of the same face, without crossing anything, splits that face in two and so increases the face count by $1$.
$K_5$ (five vertices, each joined to all the others) is non-planar.
$K_{3,3}$ (three vertices each joined to three others — the three-utilities network) is non-planar.

foundation.question_text: Explain what it means for a graph to be **planar**.
foundation.solution_text:
A graph is planar when the same vertices and edges can be arranged on a flat page so that no two edges cross.
The test is whether **some** crossing-free drawing exists, not whether the drawing in front of you happens to have crossings.
**A graph is planar if it can be drawn with no edges crossing.**

Check the drawing for crossing edges: no two tracks cross anywhere.
A drawing with no crossings already proves that a crossing-free drawing exists.
**Yes — it is planar, because it is already drawn with no edges crossing.**

One region is enclosed by the ring of five tracks.
The unbounded region outside the ring is also a face.
$1+1$
$=2$
**The drawing has $2$ faces.**

The track $BE$ divides the inside of the ring into two regions.
Adding the unbounded region outside gives one more face.
$2+1$
$=3$
**The drawing has $3$ faces.**

Regions $1$, $2$ and $3$ are each fenced in by tracks.
Region $4$ is the one region that stretches away without a boundary on the outside — the outer face.
All four regions are faces.
**Region $4$ is the outer face, and the drawing has $4$ faces.**

Drawing 2 joins $PQ$, $QR$, $RS$, $ST$, $TP$, $PR$ — the same six tracks as Drawing 1, with none added and none left out.
No two tracks in Drawing 2 cross.
**Yes — the redraw has succeeded, so the circuit is planar.**

Each of three vertices is joined to each of three others, so this network is $K_{3,3}$.
$K_{3,3}$ is one of the two standard non-planar graphs, so no rearrangement of the six vertices removes every crossing.
**No — the graph is not planar.**

development.solution_text:
Drawing 2 keeps all seven tracks, so nothing has been added or lost.
However the tracks $PR$ and $QT$ still cross one another in the middle of Drawing 2.
A successful redraw must leave no crossings at all; one of those two tracks has to be taken around the outside instead.
**No — the redraw has not succeeded, because $PR$ and $QT$ still cross.**

No two tracks cross in Drawing 2, so at first glance it looks correct.
Drawing 1 joins $WX$, $XY$, $YZ$, $ZW$, $WY$, $XZ$ — six tracks — but Drawing 2 joins only $WX$, $XY$, $WZ$, $XZ$, $YZ$ — five.
The track $WY$ has been left out, so Drawing 2 is a different network.
**No — the redraw is missing the track $WY$, so it is not a drawing of the same circuit.**

Five vertices are each joined to all four of the others, so this network is $K_5$.
$K_5$ is one of the two standard non-planar graphs, so no rearrangement of the five components removes every crossing.
**No — the graph is not planar.**

Regions $1$ and $2$ are the two rooms enclosed by doorways.
The unbounded region outside the whole plan has not been numbered, and it is also a face.
$2+1$
$=3$
**The outer region is the unnumbered face, and the drawing has $3$ faces in total.**

development.question_text:
A designer says a circuit is planar "because I moved the components around and the crossings went away", but she also deleted a track while rearranging.
Explain why her rearranged drawing does **not** show that the original circuit is planar.
development.solution_text:
A redraw is only a redraw of the same network when it keeps every vertex and every edge of the original.
Deleting a track produces a different network, and that different network may well be planar even when the original is not.
**Removing a track makes it a different graph, so a crossing-free drawing of it proves nothing about the original circuit.**

mastery.solution_text:
Each of the three machines is joined to each of the three power points, so the network is exactly $K_{3,3}$ — the same network as the three-utilities puzzle.
$K_{3,3}$ is one of the two standard non-planar graphs, alongside $K_5$, so it has **no** crossing-free drawing at all.
Moving components or bending tracks changes the picture but not the network, and every picture of a non-planar network keeps at least one crossing.
**The network is $K_{3,3}$, which is non-planar, so the designer must use a second layer (or an insulated bridge) to carry one track over another.**
